title: Evidence (law)
description: Body of facts in a legal proceeding
wiki_lead:
The law of evidence, also known as the rules of evidence, encompasses the rules and legal principles that govern the proof of facts in a legal proceeding.  These rules determine what evidence must or must not be considered by the trier of fact in reaching its decision. The trier of fact is a judge in bench trials, or the jury in any cases involving a jury.  The law of evidence is also concerned with the quantum (amount), quality, and type of proof needed to prevail in litigation. The rules vary depending upon whether the venue is a criminal court, civil court, or family court, and they vary by jurisdiction.
The quantum of evidence is the amount of evidence needed; the quality of proof is how reliable such evidence should be considered.  Important rules  that govern admissibility concern hearsay, authentication, relevance, privilege, witnesses, opinions, expert testimony, identification and rules of physical evidence.  There are various standards of evidence, standards showing how strong the evidence must be to meet the legal burden of proof in a given situation, ranging from reasonable suspicion to preponderance of the evidence, clear and convincing evidence, or beyond a reasonable doubt.
There are several types of evidence, which vary from one another in form or source.
Evidence governs the use of testimony (e.g., oral or written statements, such as an affidavit), exhibits (e.g., physical objects), documentary material, or demonstrative evidence, which are admissible (i.e., allowed to be considered by the trier of fact, such as jury) in a judicial or administrative proceeding (e.g., a court of law).
When a dispute, whether relating to a civil or criminal matter, reaches the court there will always be a number of issues which one party will have to prove in order to persuade the court to find in their favour. The law must ensure certain guidelines are set out in order to ensure that evidence presented to the court can be regarded as trustworthy.

History


Ancient and medieval law
Hammurabi's Code had some evidence requiring an oath and witness. See specifically laws 10, 11, and 12.
The Old Testament demanded at least two witnesses for conviction of a crime.
Ancient Roman law allowed freedom to judges to evaluate evidence, but insisted that "proof is incumbent on the party who affirms a fact, not on him who denies it" and "no-one should be convicted on suspicion". Medieval Roman law developed an elaborate grading of degrees of evidence. Building on the Biblical two-witness rule, it concluded that a single witness, or private documents, could constitute half-proof, which though insufficient for conviction might justify torture to extract further evidence. Because evidence in the continental (civil law) system was evaluated by judges rather than juries, that system did not develop exclusionary rules of evidence in the way English law did.


Anglophone (Common) law
A distinct feature of English common law historically was the role of the jury as a finder of fact, as opposed to the role of the judge as finder of law. The creation of modern jury trials in the 16th and 17th centuries necessitated rules of evidence to regulate what testimony and other evidence could be put before the jury.  While much of the early common law evidence rules came from judicial decisions, the English Parliament also played a role. In 1677, Parliament and the Crown enacted the Statute of Frauds and Perjuries, prohibiting plaintiffs from alleging certain contractual breaches to the jury unless accompanied by a signed, written instrument. Another early evidence rule was the prohibition on hearsay, the admission of an out-of-court statement to prove the truth of what is asserted. grok_lead: In law, evidence comprises testimony, documents, material objects, or other sensory-presented items offered in judicial proceedings to establish or refute the existence of disputed facts. Such evidence must typically demonstrate relevance by tending to make a material fact more or less probable than it would otherwise appear, while also satisfying criteria for admissibility under codified rules that exclude unduly prejudicial, unreliable, or hearsay material unless exceptions apply. The rules governing evidence, such as the Federal Rules of Evidence in the United States, form a procedural framework designed to facilitate fact-finding by triers of factâjudges or juriesâwhile balancing the pursuit of truth against risks of confusion, unfair surprise, or policy concerns like protecting informants. These rules distinguish between direct evidence, which independently proves a fact without inference (e.g., eyewitness accounts), and circumstantial evidence, which requires drawing conclusions from related facts (e.g., fingerprints at a scene). Admissibility hinges on authentication, competence, and avoidance of exclusions like character evidence offered solely to prove conduct, though privileges (e.g., attorney-client) and burdens of proof (preponderance for civil cases, beyond reasonable doubt for criminal convictions) further shape its role. Notable characteristics include ongoing debates over scientific evidence standards, such as the Daubert reliability test for expert testimony, which prioritizes empirical validation over rote acceptance, and controversies surrounding exclusionary rules that may suppress probative material to deter police misconduct. These elements underscore evidence 's foundational yet imperfect function in adversarial systems, where incomplete or contested proof can determine outcomes amid incentives for strategic withholding or fabrication.
